title: I Tore My Shoulder Chasing a Time I Never Hit — Here's What It Actually Taught Me
brief: Nemo shares her rotator cuff injury story and the nine-month recovery that reshaped her entire coaching philosophy. Personal, honest, and specific — this isn't a trauma dump, it's the origin story. End with the line: 'I built everything I have now on what I learned falling apart. That's not a warning. That's the whole point.'

draft.caption:
I Tore My Shoulder Chasing a Time I Never Hit

Junior year at UT, I was training butterfly sets at 5:45am when something gave. Not a dramatic moment — just a pop, a wrong feeling, and then nine months of watching everything I'd built around my identity slowly stop making sense.

The surgery went fine. The recovery didn't.

I'd spent my entire life treating my body like a performance machine. Optimize inputs, improve outputs. When it stopped performing, I didn't know who I was anymore. I became the most dangerous kind of injured athlete: one who was angry at her own body for failing her.

What I learned in those nine months changed everything I do as a coach:

— Pain is data, not weakness and not virtue. It's your body trying to communicate. Learn the language before you start ignoring it.

— Identity built entirely around performance is the most fragile kind. I had no floor when the performance disappeared.

— The relationship between athlete and body should not be adversarial. Mine was. Most of my clients' are. That's not a personal failing — it's what the culture teaches.

— Rest is not the absence of training. It *is* training. I had to stop believing rest was something I earned and start treating it as something I did.

I never made it back to elite competition. Eight years later, I'm grateful for that in a way I couldn't have imagined at 20.

I still swim three mornings a week. Not training. Just mine.

The injury didn't make me a better coach. The reckoning that came after it did.

I built everything I have now on what I learned falling apart. That's not a warning. That's the whole point.
